logline: A lower-caste female police officer in Rajasthan hunts a serial killer preying on women from marginalised communities, in a thriller that refuses to separate crime from caste and gender.

seasons.review_body: Dahaad arrived in May 2023 from directors Reema Kagti and Ruchika Oberoi, produced by Zoya Akhtar's Tiger Baby and Excel Entertainment, as a serial-killer thriller that treats the genre as a vehicle for caste and gender commentary rather than an end in itself. Sonakshi Sinha's Anjali Bhaati is the engine: a lower-caste officer in a system designed to discount her, chasing a killer whose victims are precisely the women that system ignores. Vijay Varma and Gulshan Devaiah round out a cast that critics singled out for ensemble cohesion. Hindustan Times called it controlled and superbly orchestrated; Film Companion highlighted the balance of commentary and entertainment. The series drew a modest 7.6 on IMDb, suggesting the thriller mechanics did not satisfy all audiences who came for pace rather than argument, but critical notices were broadly warm. The eight-episode format is efficient and the Rajasthani production design is specifically realised.

episode_reviews.title: Missing Women
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: Sub-Inspector Anjali Bhaati notices a pattern in deaths that the system has classified as suicides. The opening episode does two things at once - establishes a credible police procedural and immediately makes Anjali's caste-and-gender position a structural, not decorative, fact of the story.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Anjali filing a report nobody wants her to file - the show's thesis stated in one bureaucratic act.

critic_note.text: Dahaad is controlled and superbly orchestrated, never giving way to the sensational tone of serial killer crusades.

episode_reviews.title: The Devil Incarnate
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: A suspect comes into focus, and Anjali's persistence runs up against institutional indifference. Vijay Varma's introduction sharpens the ensemble considerably; the episode raises the threat level without resorting to a single gratuitous scene.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Anjali's first meeting with the suspect - her read on him, and the audience's, arriving at different speeds.

episode_reviews.title: Sindoora
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The serial killer's method becomes fully legible and the social architecture enabling him snaps into focus. The writing's commitment to treating caste as mechanism rather than metaphor is clearest here; the episode is the season's thematic high-water mark.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The reveal of who Sindoora actually targets - and why the system has been protecting him without knowing it.

critic_note.text: A gripping blend of social commentary and entertainment anchored by roaring performances.

episode_reviews.title: Aftermath
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The case closes but the systemic rot that enabled it does not. The finale is Reema Kagti and Ruchika Oberoi's clearest statement: justice in the procedural sense and justice in the social sense are not the same thing, and the show refuses to pretend otherwise.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Anjali's final scene - resolution that feels hard-won and incomplete at the same time, exactly as intended.
